source.title: Separating Representation from Reconstruction Enables Scalable Text Encoders
source.authors: Megi Dervishi; Mathurin Videau; Yann LeCun

record.tranche_reason: Measures held-out pretraining validation loss across compute scales, and reports downstream performance across scales for text encoders. The models and training objective differ from the original decoder-language-model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-loss scaling and downstream evaluation across compute scales. It does not report a test of small-run loss fits predicting much larger runs, separately vary parameters and tokens to estimate their loss scaling, or optimize the parameter/token split at fixed compute. It reports downstream scaling trends, not a fitted relation between pretraining loss and downstream performance.
record.test_reason: The study runs a compute scaling sweep (2e18–1e21 FLOPs, fixed 20:1 tokens-per-parameter) on masked-language-model text encoders, not decoder LMs. It reports validation-loss curves (Fig. 5) and downstream frozen and unfrozen performance against compute. That puts V1 and V6 in a new setting, so the tranche is T3, not T1. The loss evidence is qualitative only: no fitted exponents or per-run loss values.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misweighted. The central conclusion is that flat MLM encoders (BERT) yield frozen representations that become less usable as compute grows, despite improving perplexity. The authors attribute this to coupling representation with token reconstruction. Bipartite CrossBERT scales monotonically, and at large scale its frozen features beat fully finetuned baselines. The CrossBERT loss-tracking statement is a side remark offered as evidence of training stability.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a compute scaling sweep and validation loss, but on bidirectional text encoders trained with masked language modeling rather than the original decoder-language-model setup. Model size and tokens are scaled together at a fixed data-to-model ratio; the study emphasizes frozen downstream probes as well.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports higher-scale training instability and loss spikes for BERT; its discussion also notes that BERT frozen downstream degradation varies by GLUE task.

fits_no_version.finding: LR and batch-size optima follow power laws in compute (CrossBERT: LR = 564.6 C^-0.279, BSZ = 104 C^0.092), fitted on 50M–700M models and extrapolated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal training hyperparameters scale as power laws of compute for MLM encoders.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The loss scaling results are described qualitatively and plotted without numerical fitted loss exponents or reported uncertainty. Parameters and tokens are co-scaled, so their separate effects are not identified. The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and small-run extrapolation are not tested.

untested.parts: Separate parameter and token scaling with the other quantity non-bottlenecked; any fitted loss exponent.
All: no extrapolation of loss fits to larger runs (only the LR/batch-size hyperparameter power laws are extrapolated).
All: no parameter/token split is optimised; the ratio is fixed at 20:1.
Backbone shape at fixed parameter count is not tested; only predictor aspect ratio is ablated, on downstream scores, not loss.
Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss; any fitted downstream law.

missing.what: Standard BERT unfrozen (fully finetuned) MTEB performance improves with scale, in contrast with its frozen degradation
missing.locator: Section 5.3, 'Degradation of frozen BERT representations'; Figure 3

missing.what: BERT and Electra ~1B frozen GLUE collapse at 1e21 FLOPs (63.0, 66.5) versus CrossBERT 1B (81.0); Electra recovers to 80.4 with retuned hyperparameters

record.verdict_notes: The setting is bidirectional MLM encoders, so this is T3, not T1. The V1 evidence is a single qualitative sentence plus an unlabelled plot (Fig. 5); weight it lightly. The BERT downstream reversal may be confounded by large-scale training brittleness: Appendix I shows hyperparameter changes rescue Electra and partly rescue BERT 2B.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss as model size and token count scale together at a fixed 20:1 data-to-model ratio; does not isolate parameter-count or token-count scaling with the other quantities held non-bottlenecked.
Does not test whether fits from small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
Does not optimize or compare parameter/token allocations at a fixed compute budget.
Does not compare depth, width, or other backbone architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Does not test the same loss law across other modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
Tests downstream performance against compute in frozen GLUE and MTEB settings; does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
Does not assess how fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with fitting choices.

rows.subject: BERT
rows.size_stated: 76.73M to 1208.24M parameters across the scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Scaled encoder size and training tokens together and measured validation loss across compute budgets.
rows.value: The validation loss is described as tracking the expected scaling law across compute budgets; higher-scale BERT trainings also show significant instability and loss spikes.
rows.locator: Section 5.3; Section 7; Appendix F, Figure 5; Appendix I
rows.note: The paper gives no numerical fitted loss exponent or per-run loss values in the text. The curve is plotted in Figure 5; the authors separately report instability and loss spikes for higher-scale BERT.
rows.check: The text never says BERT loss follows or departs from a power law. The abstract says BERT perplexity improves with scale, and Section 5.3 reports loss spikes, but as a training-stability observation. Appendix I documents downstream collapse, not final-loss deviation. Spikes during training do not show the loss law failing, so 'partial' over-reads the text.

rows.subject: CrossBERT
rows.size_stated: 61.80M to 1176.29M parameters across the scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Scaled encoder size and training tokens together and measured validation loss across compute budgets.
rows.value: Validation loss is described as decreasing smoothly and tracking the expected scaling law at every compute budget.
rows.note: The text describes the trend but does not provide fitted loss exponents or numerical per-run loss values.
rows.check: This is a one-sentence qualitative claim made as a stability check ('tracks the expected scaling law'), with no fit or values. The state is acceptable but the evidence is weak. The locator should be Section 5.3 'Training stability', not Section 7.

rows.subject: BERT
rows.size_stated: Scaling sweep includes configurations above 500M parameters; smallest configuration is about 10× smaller than the largest configurations discussed
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated frozen-backbone GLUE performance across model scales using probes.
rows.value: For the two largest configurations (> 500M parameters), frozen performance falls below that of the smallest model in the sweep.
rows.note: The paper reports the comparison in text; it does not give the two largest models’ GLUE scores there.
rows.check: Correct per Section 5.3. Caveat: Appendix I shows the BERT ~1B collapse persists across seeds, learning rates and batch sizes, but BERT 2B* with other hyperparameters reaches 72.2. This may partly reflect training brittleness.

rows.subject: CrossBERT
rows.size_stated: Scaling sweep includes configurations from about 62M to about 1.2B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated frozen-backbone GLUE performance across model scales using probes.
rows.value: The paper describes CrossBERT as showing monotonic scaling across its evaluation metrics.
rows.note: This is a stated aggregate trend across the reported metrics; per-scale values are plotted.
rows.check: Locator fine. The monotonic claim in Section 5.3 is stated in the MTEB(eng, v2) paragraph.

relationships.reason: Authors state validation loss decreases smoothly and tracks the expected scaling law at every budget (r2). This is qualitative only, with no fit reported.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreases smoothly and tracks the expected scaling law at every tested budget.
